Chapter 10: Living with Death—Lessons for the Living
After spending years working alongside the dead, the mortician realized something unexpected. The greatest lessons she learned were all about life. For her, death wasn’t just an ending—it was more like a mirror, showing us what truly matters.
She’d hear so many stories from grieving families. Stories about love, about connection, about the small moments that made a life meaningful. And, over and over, she noticed the same truth: even when life ends, love, connection, and meaning—they stick around.
One evening, after a particularly long day, she found herself sitting with a friend who’d just lost her father. They talked quietly about regrets, about all the things that had been left unsaid. Her friend wondered, “Did I do enough? Did he really know how much I loved him?”
The mortician just listened, then gently reminded her, “Love is rarely perfect, but it’s always felt.” Most people, she explained, carry those same doubts. But in the end, it’s not really about the words we say—it’s about the love we share.
She began to treasure life’s little moments—a meal shared, a quiet walk, a simple kind word. She saw that, for so many people, what we really fear isn’t death itself. It’s the idea of not having truly lived. Her work became a daily reminder: be present, forgive, reach out.
Of course, there were days when the weight of loss felt almost too heavy to carry. But she also saw hope—hope in the way people came together. Families supporting each other, friends showing up, even strangers offering comfort.
In the face of death, life has a way of shining through—messy, beautiful, and, honestly, unbreakable.
Here’s something to remember: most of us don’t realize just how strong we are until we have to be. The mortician saw it time and time again—people finding ways to move forward. Grief never truly disappears, but it does change. It becomes part of your story, woven right into the fabric of who you are.
